extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, patent practitioners, patent-office examiners, and judges (practitioners of patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory legal treatise setting out standards for patentability, specification drafting, prosecution, priority, assignment, infringement remedies, and evidentiary & procedural rules for patents for useful inventions in the United States. Targets substantive and procedural requirements used to evaluate and produce patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject-matter: must be new and useful
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter of a patent must be new and useful (a statutory requisite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes machines, manufactures, compositions of matter, processes/arts and improvements. Cannot be mere theory or an abstract principle; must be substantially new and beneficial to society. Degree of utility is not material; relates to the whole invention. (Index refs: "SUBJECT-MATTER, must be new and useful"; pp. 1,16, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle in the abstract not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A principle, in the abstract, is not patentable; an abstract or mere purpose/effect is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An embodiment, application, or process of a principle can be patentable. The book distinguishes an abstract principle from its practical application (see "PRINCIPLE, of a machine, what is" and related entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of a principle / process as patentable subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The application of a principle, when embodied so as to produce a new and useful effect in matter, may be patentable as a process or contrivance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains when a principle becomes a process and when application of a principle constitutes patentable subject-matter (see "PRINCIPLE ... when it becomes a process; application of a principle, what constitutes").

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty: prior public use or printed publication destroys the right
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior public use or prior description in a printed/public work destroys novelty and thereby the right to a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise defines 'public use' and 'public work' and explains what kinds of prior disclosures are inconsistent with novelty (Index: "PUBLIC USE, prior, destroys right to a patent"; "PUBLIC WORK, prior description in, inconsistent with novelty").

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility as an essential statutory requisite
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility is a statutory requisite for patentability; the invention must be useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility's meaning in American law is discussed; degree of utility is not material. Failure of utility can affect the patent (see "UTILITY").

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of subject-matter required
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent must possess unity of subject-matter as required by statute; separate distinct inventions should not be claimed together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses how unity is determined, treatment of two distinct inventions, several improvements, joint inventions, and consistency with combinations (Index entries: "UNITY" and related sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of invention (not a mere substitution or obvious variant)
rubrics_metrics.description: An obvious substitution or an obvious application of known agents is not an invention; sufficiency requires more than a trivial change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats substitution, new combinations, and new applications of known agents as separate tests; explains when substitution may be patentable and when it is an obvious change (see "SUBSTITUTION" and "SUFFICIENCY OF INVENTION").

rubrics_metrics.name: New combination and new application can be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A new combination of known elements, or a new application of known agents to a new purpose, can constitute patentable subject-matter if substantially new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses combinations and applications (Index: "when a new combination"; "when a new application of known agents"). Examples and case citations illustrate when such changes suffice for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification: full, exact written description enabling practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must deposit a full and exact description in writing of the whole process, so framed that others can practise the invention from the description itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the enabling/written-description principle explained in Preliminary Observations and the SPECIFICATIONS sections: must state how to practice, state best mode, and be sufficient for persons of ordinary skill to practise without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must agree with the patent (no repugnancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications must agree with the patent; repugnancy between specification and patent affects validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise warns against discrepancies between the specification and the patent (Index: 'REPUGNANCY, between specifications and patent, effect of'; see §§ cited on specification drafting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must not be ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications must not be ambiguous; ambiguous terms and omissions are common defects that can invalidate a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index and chapters list ambiguous terms, omission of necessary descriptions, incorrect drawings, and misleading content as defects under English and American law (see 'SPECIFICATIONS — common defects' and detailed headings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must distinguish old from new
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must distinguish what is old in the art from what is new in the inventor's contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance on how to describe what is old and what is novel; avoid claiming what is not original and do not mislead the public about novelty (see 'must distinguish what is old from what is new').

rubrics_metrics.name: State the best mode of producing the effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should state the best mode known to the patentee of producing the claimed effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple references (e.g., 'to state the best mode of producing an effect') stress disclosure of the best or preferred method to practise the invention; failure may be ground to invalidate or limit the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressed to persons of competent skill (skilled artisan standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications are to be addressed to persons of competent skill in the art — i.e., technical description may assume ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May contain technical terms; instructions should be sufficient for a skilled person; discussion of where experimentation is or is not permissible (Index refs: "addressed to persons of competent skill").

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings are part of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings annexed to the specification form part of the specification and are used to explain the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why drawings are necessary, how they should be prepared, and that incorrect drawings are a common defect (see 'drawings annexed to, a part of'; 'why to be accompanied with drawings').

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification should not contain useless descriptions or mislead the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications must not contain useless descriptions and must not mislead the public about the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes examples of misleading inclusions and instructions to avoid irrelevant material that might obscure the inventive contribution (see 'must not contain useless descriptions'; 'must not mislead the public').

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification should describe every thing essential
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should describe every thing essential to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must describe essential elements and materials; guidance on when materials need be stated and when they need not; slight defects may render patent void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification may contain technical terms but must not misuse terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical terminology is permissible but terms should be used correctly — misuse of technical terms can be fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise emphasizes correct technical usage to avoid ambiguity and misdescription (see 'may contain technical terms' and 'must not misuse terms').

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification may be liberally construed but is judged by the court/jury
rubrics_metrics.description: While specifications may be liberally construed, courts (and sometimes juries) determine their meaning in litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatise discusses construction principles and the respective roles of court and jury in interpreting specifications (see 'to be construed by the court' and 'how far to be judged of by the jury').

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification should not require undue experiment; limited experiments may be allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification should not require undue experiments to practise the invention; however, in some cases limited experiments may properly be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains when experiments are improper vs when reasonable experimentation may be expected; references on 'must not require experiments' and 'when may require experiments'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments & disclaimers allowed by statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to specifications and disclaimers are permitted by statute under specified conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes statutory processes for amendment and use of disclaimers to narrow claims; procedural guidance and common defects related to amendments are discussed (see 'amendments of, allowed by statute' and 'by disclaimers').

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims / Profert of letters-patent in pleadings
rubrics_metrics.description: The profert of letters-patent is to be made in the declaration and has effects in litigation and bills for injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance on how patents and the contents of the letters-patent are used in pleadings and in equity suits (see 'PROFERT OF LETTERS-PATENT').

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use and printed publication standards (what counts as public)
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatise sets standards for what constitutes prior public use and what qualifies as a printed/public work for novelty purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed discussion (§§ referenced) on different forms of prior disclosure (public exhibition, sales, publications) and how they affect novelty and priority (see 'PUBLIC USE' and 'PUBLIC WORK').

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof to show infringement lies on the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains evidentiary burdens in proving infringement and related issues in actions at law (Index: 'burden of proof, to show infringement, on plaintiff').

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of reduction to practice and inventorship: fabricator vs inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabrication of a machine by a workman for another is prima facie evidence the fabricator made it; but employment and direction by another rebuts the inference — reduction to practice and inventorship depend on surrounding facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples (Goodyear/Warner, etc.) illustrate that producing a machine for an employer does not necessarily make the fabricator the inventor; the burden may shift to show who conceived the invention and who directed its making (see Judge Cranch decisions excerpt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be patentee; persons entitled to take, renew, or extend patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatise specifies who may be a patentee under statute (including treatment of aliens), and discusses persons entitled to take, renew, or extend patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes treatment of joint inventors, assignments, licenses, and relations between patentees and licensees in regard to validity (see 'The Persons entitled to take, renew, or extend Patents' and related index entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments and licenses: transmission of interest; recording
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules on assignments and licenses govern transmission of the interest in letters-patent; recording of assignments and when proof of recording may be given in actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses effect of assignments, recording procedures, proof in litigation, and how assignments affect standing and remedies (see 'Transmission of the Interest in Letters-Patent' and 'RECORDING OF ASSIGNMENT').

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceedings to obtain patent: petition, oath, fees, signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural requirements include the petition, oath, payment of fees, and requisite signatures of Secretary of State and Commissioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also covers caveat for incomplete invention, treatment of interfering applications, renewal & amendment procedures, and the Patent Office organization and officers (see Part II contents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat for incomplete invention and interfering applications
rubrics_metrics.description: A caveat is available for incomplete inventions; interfering applications procedures resolve priority disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes when a caveat may be filed and the handling of interfering applications and appeals to the courts (see Part II headings and case law references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal and extension of patents: statutory allowances and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Renewal (surrender & reissue/renewal) and statutory extensions are permitted under specified conditions and subject to statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains statutory grounds for renewal/extension, how surrender and reissue operate, and the role of the Patent Office and courts in such proceedings (see 'RENEWAL' entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement remedies: action at law & equity; injunctions; damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies for infringement include actions at law (damages) and equity (injunctions/accounts); rules of damages and equitable relief are discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed chapters on infringement, the remedy by action at law, and remedies in equity (see Part IV chapters). Includes jurisdictional issues and procedural considerations for injunctions (e.g., quia timet) and accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence: how patents and specifications are used as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules on how the specification of a former patent is read in actions for infringement and what evidence is required in patent litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes who may be competent or incompetent witnesses (e.g., patentees, licensees), how to prove priority and reduction to practice, and burden allocations (see 'EVIDENCE' and related index entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of damages & rule for awarding damages for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a rule of damages for infringement discussed in the treatise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter guidance sets out methods for calculating damages in infringement suits; see Index 'RULE OF DAMAGES' and relevant chapter sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: When invention may be an art (process) vs other categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of when the subject-matter may be an art (process) versus a machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains tests and examples distinguishing processes from other categories and when an application of a principle qualifies as an art (see 'SUBJECT-MATTER' classification and 'PROCESS' entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Must not claim purely inchoate ideas or elementary principles
rubrics_metrics.description: An inchoate idea, elementary principle, or a discovery in pure science unconnected to practical application is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise gives examples and doctrinal reasoning distinguishing scientific discovery from patentable practical application (see 'cannot be an inchoate idea', 'an elementary principle', 'a science').

rubrics_metrics.name: When to state materials and how to procure substances
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification guidance on when the patentee should state materials used in a machine and when to state how substances may be procured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains when material composition must be disclosed and when procurement methods must be explained (see 'when to state materials of a machine' and 'when to state how substances may be procured').

rubrics_metrics.name: Slight defects in specifications may render patent void
rubrics_metrics.description: Even slight defects in a specification may render the patent void under some circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatise catalogs common defects and their consequences; emphasizes care in specification drafting to avoid invalidation (see 'slight defects in, may render patent void').

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint inventions and servitude/employee-created work: inventor vs employer
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal criteria distinguish between an inventor and a workman/servant who fabricates an invention at the request, direction, and expense of another; the employer may be the inventor in law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples explain the presumption that a machine made for an employer was made according to the employer's directions, shifting burden to the fabricator to show otherwise (Judge Cranch decisions excerpt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording and publication duties of the Patent Office; lists and dating
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Office duties include making & publishing lists of patents, recording assignments anew under some conditions, and rules about dating patents (including back-dating in certain cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural entries and index items set out when and how the Office handles lists, re-recordings, and dating issues (see 'PATENT OFFICE' and related index entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional limits and appellate review in patent causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatise sets out jurisdiction of Congress and federal courts and appellate review procedures, including Supreme Court review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses the appellate power in patent causes and when writs of error lie to the Supreme Court (see 'Jurisdiction of Congress and the Federal Courts' and 'WRIT OF ERROR' index entries).
